items.stem: The League of Nations was set up in January 1920 with its headquarters in Geneva. Describe the organisation of the League of Nations.
items.answer: The Assembly met once a year and every member had one vote. The Council met several times a year and in emergencies; it had permanent members such as Britain and France. The Secretariat was a civil service that kept records and organised the League's work. The Permanent Court of International Justice at The Hague settled legal disputes. Commissions and agencies dealt with refugees, health, slavery, mandates and working conditions (the ILO).

items.stem: The League of Nations was set up in January 1920 with its headquarters in Geneva. (a) What were the aims of the League of Nations? [4] (b) Why did the USA not join the League of Nations? [6]
items.answer: (a) To discourage aggression and keep the peace through collective security. To encourage countries to cooperate, especially in business and trade. To encourage disarmament. To improve living and working conditions of people around the world. (b) The Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles, which included the League Covenant. Many Americans wanted isolationism after heavy losses in a European war. They feared Article 10 might force the USA to send troops to defend other countries. Some thought membership would harm American trade, for example through sanctions. Party politics: Republicans opposed the Democrat Wilson.

items.stem: The League of Nations was set up in January 1920 with its headquarters in Geneva. ‘The absence of the USA was the main weakness of the League of Nations.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Without the USA, sanctions were weak because aggressors could trade with America. The League lacked the world's most powerful economy and potential military power. Against: Unanimity and slow procedures made decisions difficult. The League had no army. Britain and France put their own interests first, as at Corfu and Abyssinia. The Depression made countries less willing to act. Judgement: The USA's absence weakened sanctions, but the League failed mainly because its leading members, Britain and France, would not act firmly.

items.stem: What happened in the dispute between Greece and Bulgaria in 1925?
items.answer: Greek soldiers were killed in an incident on the border with Bulgaria. Greece invaded Bulgaria. Bulgaria appealed to the League. The League ordered Greece to withdraw and pay compensation. Greece obeyed, though it complained that larger powers were treated differently.

items.stem: The League of Nations had both successes and failures in the 1920s. (a) Describe the League's humanitarian work in the 1920s. [4] (b) Why was the League able to settle the Aaland Islands dispute? [6]
items.answer: (a) About 400,000 prisoners of war were returned home. The Refugee Committee helped refugees, for example with Nansen passports. The Health Committee worked against diseases such as leprosy and malaria. The Slavery Commission helped free 200,000 slaves in Sierra Leone. The ILO campaigned for better working conditions. Loans helped Austria and Hungary to recover. (b) Sweden and Finland were both small powers that respected the League. Both sides agreed to accept the League's decision. The League's solution protected the Swedish-speaking islanders by demilitarising the islands and guaranteeing their culture. No Great Power interest was threatened.

items.stem: ‘The League of Nations was successful in the 1920s.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: It settled disputes over the Aaland Islands (1921), Upper Silesia (1921) and between Greece and Bulgaria (1925). Its agencies returned prisoners of war, helped refugees and fought disease and slavery. Germany joined in 1926, strengthening it. Against: It failed over Vilna (1920) and Corfu (1923), when larger powers used force. Major agreements such as Locarno and Kellogg-Briand were made outside it. It made little progress on disarmament. Judgement: The League was successful when dealing with small powers and humanitarian problems, but it failed when a larger power was involved.

items.stem: How important was the work of the League's agencies compared with its work on disputes? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Agencies helped millions: refugees, prisoners of war, freed slaves and disease control. Their work continued after 1945 in UN bodies such as the ILO and the WHO. Against: The League's main aim was to prevent war, so disputes were the real test. Successes in disputes, such as Bulgaria 1925, built confidence in collective security. Agency work could not prevent the aggression of the 1930s. Judgement: The agencies achieved the most lasting successes, but the League's reputation depended on keeping the peace, so disputes were more important to its overall success.

items.stem: The League's structure made it slow to take decisions. Describe the weaknesses in the League's organisation.
items.answer: Decisions in the Council and Assembly had to be unanimous. The Council met only a few times a year, so it reacted slowly. The League had no army of its own. Sanctions depended on members being willing to apply them. Important countries were missing, such as the USA.

items.stem: Critics argued that the League of Nations was a “toothless tiger”. Describe the steps the League could take against an aggressor.
items.answer: It could investigate and hold an enquiry, for example the Lytton Commission. It could condemn the aggressor (moral condemnation). It could impose economic sanctions such as banning trade. It could, in theory, ask members to provide troops for military action.

items.stem: ‘The League failed because of the weaknesses in its organisation.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Unanimity and infrequent meetings made it slow and indecisive. It had no army to enforce decisions. Sanctions were weak without the USA. Against: Britain and France's self-interest and unwillingness to act was decisive, as over Abyssinia. The Depression made countries more aggressive and less willing to cooperate. Determined aggressors like Japan and Italy simply left the League. Judgement: Organisational weaknesses made failure more likely, but the League failed mainly because its leading members lacked the will to use the powers it had.

items.answer: (a) The League condemned Italy as the aggressor. It imposed economic sanctions in October-November 1935. Sanctions did not include oil, coal or steel. Sanctions were half-hearted and excluded oil. Britain and France were seen to betray the League with the Hoare-Laval Pact. It showed collective security had failed, encouraging Hitler, who remilitarised the Rhineland in March 1936.

items.stem: The crises in Manchuria and Abyssinia exposed the weaknesses of the League of Nations. ‘The Abyssinian crisis was more damaging to the League than the Manchurian crisis.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Abyssinia was in Europe's sphere of interest, close to British and French routes, so the League could have acted. Britain and France openly undermined the League with the Hoare-Laval Pact. It destroyed faith in sanctions and encouraged Hitler. Against: Manchuria was the first major test, and failure showed a Great Power could defy the League. Japan's departure in 1933 weakened the League. Manchuria set the pattern of delay and inaction. Judgement: Manchuria exposed the League's weakness, but Abyssinia was more damaging because the League had the means to act and its leading members chose not to.

Disagree / other factors: Manchuria was the first major test, and failure showed a Great Power could defy the League. Japan's departure in 1933 weakened the League. items.stem: The Covenant of the League of Nations was written into all the peace treaties of 1919-20. How far was the League of Nations doomed to failure from the start? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: The USA never joined, and Germany and the USSR were excluded at first. It had no army and needed unanimous decisions. It was linked to the hated peace treaties. Against: It had successes in the 1920s, such as the Aaland Islands and Bulgaria. Its agencies helped refugees and fought disease. Its failures came mainly in the 1930s, after the Depression. Judgement: The League had serious weaknesses from the start, but it was the Depression and the aggression of major powers in the 1930s that exposed them.

items.stem: How far was collective security a realistic idea? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: It worked against small powers in the 1920s. All members accepted it in the Covenant. Against: It required countries to risk war for distant states in which they had no interest. It needed all the Great Powers to be members, which never happened. In the 1930s Great Powers were the aggressors. Judgement: Collective security was realistic only if the Great Powers were committed to it, which they were not.

items.answer: For: It encouraged aggression by Japan and Italy and helped Hitler to power. It made Britain and France unwilling to impose sanctions or spend on rearmament. items.stem: What was the Hoare-Laval Pact?
items.answer: It was a secret plan made in December 1935 by the British and French foreign ministers. It would have given Italy about two-thirds of Abyssinia. It was leaked to the press. There was public outrage in Britain and Hoare resigned. It showed Britain and France were undermining the League.
